name: Hackle (wig preparation)

lead: A hackle is a wig-making tool: a metal plate with rows of pointed needles, usually clamped to a table. Hair is pulled through it to separate and straighten strands.
For appearance, it produces smoother, more even hair for custom wigs and extensions, including 'double drawn' hair in which all strands are a similar length for a fuller look at the ends.

paras: Wig makers draw bundles of hair through the needles to blend colors, untangle wigs and extensions, and prepare hair for single or double drawn wigs. Single drawn removes the shortest root hairs; double drawn sorts a bundle so strands match in length.
The needles are sharp and can cause puncture injuries, so the plate is typically fixed to a table. It is a professional workshop tool rather than a styling product.

angle.text: Wig makers use the hackle to prepare hair before it is knotted into a wig. The result is hair with consistent length and blended color.

lead: A hackle, also spelled heckle, is a wig-making tool consisting of a metal plate with rows of pointed needles used to blend or straighten hair. It is typically clamped to a table and is a preliminary step in custom wig making [1].

It helps looks indirectly: the prepared hair gives wigs and extensions blended colors, fewer tangles and more uniform lengths. Double drawn hair, made by drawing a bundle through the hackle to separate different lengths, is more expensive because it uses much more single drawn hair [1].
infobox: Metal plate with rows of pointed needles

paras: The tool is a plate studded with very sharp needles, clamped to a table [1]. Uses include blending hairs into custom color mixtures, untangling wigs or extensions, and preparing hair for single or double drawn wigs [1].

In single drawn hair the shortest hairs at the root are removed. In double drawn hair a bundle is drawn through the hackle to separate hairs of different lengths so the finished strands are of equal length [1].
The word also names a comb used to dress flax, hemp and jute fibers, from Middle English hakell, linked to a word for hook [2].
